## Introduction

<!-- One or two paragraphs: what question are you looking at and why does it
matter? -->

State the problem. For example: how much extra selection intensity do you
actually buy by selecting a smaller fraction of your population?

## Background

<!-- Optional. Inline math goes between single dollar signs; a display equation
between double dollar signs. LaTeX syntax:
https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Mathematical_expressions -->

Selection intensity $i$ is the mean of the selected group in standard deviation
units. For a selected proportion $p$ under a normal distribution,

$$
i = \frac{\phi(z)}{p}, \qquad z = \Phi^{-1}(1 - p),
$$

where $\phi$ and $\Phi$ are the standard normal density and CDF.

## Analysis

<!-- In .Rmd, chunk options go inside the braces: the first word is the label,
then fig.cap=, warning=, echo=FALSE (hide code), eval=FALSE (show but don't
run). Always set a seed for anything random. -->

```{r fig-selection-intensity, fig.cap="Selection intensity as a function of the selected proportion", warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)

selected_fraction <- seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)
z <- qnorm(1 - selected_fraction)
intensity <- dnorm(z) / selected_fraction

df <- data.frame(selected_fraction = selected_fraction, intensity = intensity)

ggplot(df, aes(x = selected_fraction, y = intensity)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "#2f4a3c") +
  labs(x = "Fraction selected", y = "Selection intensity (i)") +
  theme_minimal()
```
